conflicts.point: Whether mechanistic interpretability tools can reliably map and predict frontier AI model behavior at scale without creating insurmountable administrative and resource barriers for non-incumbent researchers.

positions.stance: Circuit-mapping tools successfully expose internal planning structures and feature superposition in complex transformer models, providing essential pre-deployment safeguards when supported by public funding.

Transformer weights represent distributed probabilistic patterns rather than deterministic physical structures, rendering internal weight audits ineffective and overly burdensome for independent researchers.

conflicts.point: Whether federal grant reallocations toward mechanistic interpretability prevent regulatory capture or instead reinforce incumbent market power by imposing compliance costs on smaller labs.

positions.stance: Targeting National Science Foundation and Department of Energy grants specifically toward interpretability research democratizes safety verification by equipping academic labs with necessary resources.
Grant application requirements and compliance overhead systematically favor well-resourced legacy labs with existing compute infrastructure, concentrating market power.

verdicts.conflict: Whether mechanistic interpretability tools can reliably map and predict frontier AI model behavior at scale without creating insurmountable administrative and resource barriers for non-incumbent researchers.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist position prevails because empirical demonstrations of feature superposition and circuit mapping in transformer models confirm that internal structures can be isolated. The accelerationist claim relies on theoretical limits of distributed patterns without addressing recent successes in modular circuit identification.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Published evidence showing that scaling models above specific parameter thresholds renders current circuit-mapping tools mathematically impossible or statistically insignificant would flip this verdict.

verdicts.conflict: Whether federal grant reallocations toward mechanistic interpretability prevent regulatory capture or instead reinforce incumbent market power by imposing compliance costs on smaller labs.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist position prevails by identifying specific funding mechanisms through the National Science Foundation and Department of Energy that bypass commercial compliance structures. The skeptic argument assumes all interpretability mandates function as burdensome regulations rather than direct research grants.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical documentation proving that National Science Foundation and Department of Energy grant structures systematically direct funds to incumbent firms rather than academic researchers would reverse this evaluation.
